Figure 1B: is the corrected increase from 158 to 182 red sites unusual?¶

This notebook reconstructs Figure 1B of Karbacher et al. and asks how unusual the after-minus-before increase of +24 is under participant reassignment.

Update recorded on 31 October 2026: an author identified reversed visit labels for donors 5 and 8. Reversing those four labels gives 158 before and 182 after, matching the published counts. Every shuffled model has been refitted with the corrected visits. The historical 158/176, p = 0.2630 run remains archived and is compared below; it is not the current result.

The correction is an explicit local patch to the archived annotations. It is not a downloaded replacement sample sheet. See the correction note and four array-level changes.

Status: unrestricted diagnostic with unresolved diet mapping. The numeric 24/24 grouping is retained, and groups remain code 0 and code 1. Named diet annotations conflict. Original allocation-block membership is unavailable, so unrestricted participant shuffles cannot reproduce the original blocked allocation.

We keep methylation measurements fixed, use the same participant assignment across both visits and every CpG, refit limma, and count sites passing the same thresholds. Run All checks saved results; it does not perform thousands of new fits. The README documents the complete pipeline.

1. Observed red-site counts¶

A site is red when it meets both original rules: limma raw two-sided $p < 0.05$ and $|\Delta M| > 0.5$. Every shuffled analysis uses these same rules. These are counts of thresholded CpGs, rather than genome-wide discoveries after multiple-testing correction. The effect scale and candidate model are explained below.

2. Test the change: after minus before¶

At each visit $v$, count sites passing the original red-site rule:

$$C_v = \sum_{j=1}^{812934} \mathbf{1}\{p^{\mathrm{limma}}_{j,v}<0.05 \;\mathrm{and}\;|\Delta M_{j,v}|>0.5\}.$$

Our statistic is the signed count change:

$$D = C_{\mathrm{after}}-C_{\mathrm{before}},\qquad D_{\mathrm{observed}}=182-158=24.$$

The saved simulation refitted the corrected data 9,999 times, using seed 70899:

  1. Keep all methylation measurements fixed.
  2. Randomly reassign the 48 participants to two groups of 24.
  3. Apply the same assignment to both visits and every CpG. Each person's before/after pair stays together, and the relationships between CpGs are preserved.
  4. Refit the same four group-by-visit means and re-estimate limma's empirical Bayes variance prior. Apply exactly the same raw-p and effect thresholds.
  5. Record the before and after red-site counts for that assignment.

We now subtract those counts within each saved row to obtain $D_b$. No new model fits are needed. We do not independently shuffle visits or mix counts from different assignments. To ask whether the observed increase is unusually large, use

$$p_{\mathrm{increase}} =\frac{1+\#\{D_b\ge24\}}{9999+1}.$$

This is a one-sided upper-tail test, including ties. The added 1 accounts for the observed assignment in the Monte Carlo calculation. The site-level limma p-values inside the red-site rule remain two-sided. This answers the question about an increase; testing unusually large changes in either direction would require a two-sided statistic.

The histogram is zoomed to changes between −200 and 200; its footnote gives the number outside this view. All 9,999 changes contribute to the p-value, regardless of the displayed range. The red line marks +24; dark bars show increases of +24 or more. Each shuffle uses its own baseline count, so this is not conditional on starting at exactly 158 and is not the probability of the exact pair 158 → 182. The middle 95% range describes shuffled changes, not a confidence interval for a diet effect.

Allocation assumption: these are unrestricted fixed-size shuffles. Original trial methods report block randomization (block size 13). Verified diet assignments, participant-to-block mapping and the allocation procedure for the methylation subset are unavailable. Thus the present calculation is conditional on joint exchangeability of whole participant profiles, not an exact randomization test under the documented trial design. Blocks cannot be recovered just by splitting sorted participant IDs into groups of 13. The relevance of exchangeability restrictions is discussed in the permutation inference reference.

null_counts = pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv")
B = len(null_counts)
assert B == run["repetitions"]
# Subtract within each assignment: before and after share the same participant grouping.
changes = null_counts["after"] - null_counts["before"]
observed_change = int(summary.loc["after", "highlighted"] - summary.loc["before", "highlighted"])
extreme_changes = int((changes >= observed_change).sum())
change_p = (1 + extreme_changes) / (B + 1)

# Independently check the saved summary and paired export before displaying them.
saved_changes = pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_changes.csv")
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes["shuffle"], np.arange(1, B+1))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes[["before", "after"]], null_counts[["before", "after"]])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes["change"], changes)
saved_change_test = pd.read_csv(OUT / "change_test_summary.csv").iloc[0]
assert observed_change == saved_change_test.observed_change
assert extreme_changes == saved_change_test.shuffles_ge_observed
assert np.isclose(change_p, saved_change_test.change_p_upper)

change_results = pd.DataFrame([{

    "Shuffle median change": changes.median(),
    "Shuffled 2.5%": changes.quantile(0.025),
    "Shuffled 97.5%": changes.quantile(0.975),
    "Shuffles ≥ observed change": extreme_changes,
    "Total shuffles": B,

}], index=["After − before"])

3. Separate count tests at each visit¶

For context, we can ask whether the observed total count at either visit is unusually large. These are secondary diagnostics, distinct from the change test above. Using the same 9,999 assignments, compare each visit's count with its observed count:

$$p_{\mathrm{count},v} =\frac{1+\#\{C_{v,b}\ge C_{v,\mathrm{observed}}\}}{9999+1}.$$

The site-level limma test remains two-sided; these count tests are upper-tailed. They ask about an excess of red sites. The two visit-specific p-values are shown separately, without an across-visit adjustment.

The histograms show shuffled counts with a red line at each observed count. Dark bars are the upper tails used for the p-values. Their middle 95% ranges describe shuffled counts, not confidence intervals for diet effects. A few paired counts are also shown.

    # Keep limma p-values inside the red-site rule. Only the total count is tested here.

    count_p = (1 + extreme) / (B + 1)
    assert extreme == saved_count_test.loc[time, "shuffles_ge_observed"]

4. Which annotations are corrected, and which remain unresolved?¶

The visit patch changes only four time labels for donors 5 and 8. Participant IDs, measurements, array order and group assignments are unchanged. The public annotation files were still identical to the archived copies on 31 October 2026; see the public-file check.

The numeric diet field contains 24/24 participants, while the named field contains 26 vegan and 22 meat-rich participants. Both fields are constant within a person's pair, but they define different groupings. The author confirms 24 participants per diet, although the full verified sample-to-diet mapping has not yet been supplied. The analysis continues to use code 0 minus code 1 without assigning diet names.

The author also confirms sex-annotation errors and totals of 30 women and 18 men. Individual corrections were not provided. Consequently the retained public labels still contain 32 women and 16 men. Sex does not enter the initial Figure 1B model; these labels cannot be used to reproduce the author's later age/sex-adjusted model without clarification.

Descriptive sample-distance QC is recorded in the corrected audit. It does not establish biological identity, identify sample swaps, or justify exclusions.

5. What “fold change” means in this reconstruction¶

A beta value $β$ describes methylation on a scale from 0 to 1. Our reconstruction uses the transformed value

$$M=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\right), \qquad \Delta M=\overline M_{\mathrm{code\ 0}}-\overline M_{\mathrm{code\ 1}}.$$

The saved limma column logFC contains $\Delta M$. Consequently, $2^{\Delta M}$ is the ratio of geometric mean methylation odds between the two groups. An effect of 0.5 corresponds to an odds ratio of $\sqrt{2}\approx1.414$. It is not a 50-percentage-point change, nor a ratio of arithmetic mean beta values. The author confirmed M-value input. We derive M-values from the public processed beta matrix; the original M-value matrix has not been supplied.

The author confirmed the initial four-group-by-time-mean model. Our R fit includes all five supplied contrasts; we use code 0 minus code 1 at each visit for Figure 1B. The candidate model has 92 residual degrees of freedom and no participant blocking. limma moderates the site variances by borrowing information across CpGs, making individual variance estimates less unstable. Its parametric p-values then use a moderated t reference distribution. This is not the ordinary Welch t-test.

The two visits are correlated within a person. The original candidate limma model does not explicitly model that correlation; the participant shuffles preserve the pairs. Both visit-specific contrasts are between-group comparisons. They do not directly test whether the two groups changed differently from baseline.

  • Bottom row: one participant reassignment from the example seed shown below. The same reassignment is applied to both visits and every CpG. The same R/limma script refits the model and variance moderation.

Its saved p-values and fitted effects are checked against the red-site counts. The example seed can be changed independently of the full count-test seed.

The p-values on the vertical axes are the limma p-values fitted within each displayed grouping. The bottom row provides a visual sanity check. The change-test histogram in section 2 uses all 9,999 assignments to assess the increase of +24. The separate visit-specific count diagnostics are in section 3. Both rows use the corrected visit labels for donors 5 and 8. The earlier example counts and figures remain in the archived original-annotation results.

7. What the corrected change test establishes¶

The reconstructed increase is 182 − 158 = +24 red sites. Of 9,999 joint participant shuffles, 1,880 give an increase of at least +24, yielding an upper-tail permutation p-value of 0.1881 with the +1 correction. The shuffled median is +1, with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles -91.05 and +95. The Monte Carlo standard error is approximately 0.0039.

The increase is not unusual under the retained numeric grouping and unrestricted shuffle scheme. This differs from the archived +18, p = 0.2630 analysis because both the observed counts and every shuffled fit now use corrected visits. It is not a calculation that applies the new +24 cutoff to the old distribution.

Each difference uses paired counts from one assignment. The test preserves relationships between visits and CpGs. A net increase of 24 need not mean exactly 24 new sites became red: sites can enter and leave the red set. It does not identify individual effects or test a diet-by-time interaction at individual CpGs.

Exchangeability applies to whole before/after profiles. Equal average changes alone are insufficient to justify these shuffles. The statistic and upper-tail direction were chosen during exploratory review. A large p-value neither establishes equivalent diets nor rules out methylation effects.

Both published counts now match, and the initial model structure is confirmed by the author. Diet mapping, allocation blocks, original input M-values and site-level identity still require clarification. This added count-change p-value does not show that published individual-CpG p-values are incorrect. Original IDAT normalization, probe filtering, and the paper's other outcomes are outside this analysis.

The corrected audit verifies the four changes, retained source hashes, saved summaries and independent factorial-coded R fits for observed and selected shuffled assignments. Original audit evidence remains in results/audit and applies to the earlier scenario.

Numerical verification and Monte Carlo stability

All 14 automated tests pass, including comparisons with R/limma, numerical edge cases, participant alignment, the explicit correction, rejection of applying it twice, and input-file integrity checks. On the corrected full data, the invariance audit checks explicit residual calculations, swapping group names, reversing visits, reordering participants, and distances from classification cutoffs.

A separate 9,999-shuffle run with seed 70901 checks Monte Carlo stability using the corrected visits. It gives p = 0.1859, compared with 0.1881 for seed 70899. It does not replace or pool with the primary run. The table below independently recalculates both upper tails. The original-annotation results are shown separately, using their own observed +18 and original distribution.

import hashlib

# Independently recompute each tail from its own paired rows.
check_run = json.loads((ROOT / "results/corrected_visits/audit/independent_seed_summary.json").read_text())

assert check_run["seed"] != run["seed"]
assert check_run["annotation_scenario"] == run["annotation_scenario"]
assert check_run["samples_sha256"] == run["samples_sha256"]
assert len(check_counts) == check_run["repetitions"]
assert hashlib.sha256((OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv").read_bytes()).hexdigest() == check_run["original_count_sha256"]

stability = []
for label, seed, pairs in [
    ("Corrected visits: primary", run["seed"], pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv")),
    ("Corrected visits: verification", check_run["seed"], check_counts),
]:

8. Sensitivity to the annotation field and model design¶

These rows use either the numeric field or the conflicting named field. They also compare the four-cell model, which pools residual variance across visits, with a separate fit at each visit. They are recorded alternatives, not settings tuned to recover the published count. The later subject-blocked model mentioned in the paper is not reconstructed here.

The named-label scenario uses different participant assignments and unequal group sizes. Any BH findings in that scenario cannot validate a vegan-versus-meat effect while the annotations remain unresolved. All sensitivity rows below use the same four corrected visit labels.

sensitivity = []
for field, label in [("diet_code", "Numeric codes (24 / 24)"),

    pooled = pd.read_csv(folder / "limma_summary.csv").set_index("time")
    separate = pd.read_csv(folder / "separate_time_sensitivity.csv").set_index("time")

                                  ("Separate visits", separate, (0, 1))]:

            "Before highlighted": int(table.loc[indices[0], "highlighted"]),
            "After highlighted": int(table.loc[indices[1], "highlighted"]),
            "Before BH < 0.05": int(table.loc[indices[0], "bh_below_005"]),
            "After BH < 0.05": int(table.loc[indices[1], "bh_below_005"])})

9. Inspect an individual CpG from the limma analysis¶

This optional example shows the measurements behind one point in the observed volcano plots. Set SITE below to a CpG ID and rerun the example. With SITE = None, we select the red follow-up site with the smallest limma p-value. This is a descriptive selection after inspecting the results, not independent confirmation of an effect.

The table shows the fitted M-value difference, original raw limma p-value, and its Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment over all CpGs at that visit. No site in the numeric grouping has a BH-adjusted p-value below 0.05. Red sites follow the figure's raw-p and effect rule; they are not genome-wide discoveries after multiple-testing correction.

The plots show each participant's measured beta values and group means. Each person appears in both panels. These beta means are descriptive; the fitted effect uses M-values.

columns = ["cpg", "logFC", "t", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val"]
results = {
    time: pd.read_csv(OUT / f"{time}_limma.csv.gz", usecols=columns).set_index("cpg")
    for time in TIMES
}
for time, table in results.items():
    assert len(table) == audit["matrix_shape"][0] and table.index.is_unique
    assert np.isfinite(table.to_numpy()).all()
    for pcol in ("P.Value", "adj.P.Val"):
        assert table[pcol].between(0, 1).all()
    table["highlighted"] = (table.logFC.abs() > EFFECT_CUTOFF) & (table["P.Value"] < ALPHA)
    assert int(table.highlighted.sum()) == summary.loc[time, "highlighted"]

SITE = None  # Replace with an ID such as "cg14817997" to inspect another site.
if SITE is None:
    candidates = results["after"].loc[results["after"].highlighted, "P.Value"]
    SITE = candidates.idxmin() if len(candidates) else results["after"]["P.Value"].idxmin()
if not all(SITE in table.index for table in results.values()):
    raise KeyError(f"CpG {SITE!r} is absent from the result tables")

display(Markdown(f"**Selected CpG: `{SITE}`**"))
site_table = pd.DataFrame({time.title(): table.loc[SITE, [
    "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val", "highlighted"
]] for time, table in results.items()}).T.rename(columns={
    "logFC": "ΔM (0 − 1)", "P.Value": "limma raw p", "adj.P.Val": "limma BH-adjusted p",
    "highlighted": "Red under original rule",
})
display(site_table)

beta_path = ROOT / "data/processed/beta.bin"
if beta_path.exists():
    shape = tuple(audit["matrix_shape"])
    assert beta_path.stat().st_size == np.prod(shape) * 8
    # Check the explicit CpG ordering before looking up any beta values.
    cpg_ids = pd.Index((ROOT / "data/processed/cpg_ids.txt").read_text().splitlines())
    assert cpg_ids.equals(results["before"].index) and cpg_ids.equals(results["after"].index)
    row = cpg_ids.get_loc(SITE)
    beta = np.memmap(beta_path, dtype="<f8", mode="r", shape=shape)
    observed = samples.copy()
    observed["beta"] = np.array(beta[row])
    del beta
    jitter_rng = np.random.default_rng(70899)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    for time, ax in enumerate(axes):
        for x, (group, color) in enumerate((("0", "#208c72"), ("1", "#cc7847"))):
            values = observed.loc[(observed.time == time) & (observed.diet_code == group), "beta"]
            ax.scatter(x + jitter_rng.uniform(-0.09, 0.09, len(values)), values,
                       color=color, s=25, alpha=0.8)
            ax.hlines(values.mean(), x-0.18, x+0.18, color="black", lw=2)
        ax.set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=["Code 0", "Code 1"],
               xlim=(-0.5, 1.5), ylim=(0, 1), title=TIMES[time].title(), ylabel="Beta value")
    fig.suptitle(f"{SITE} — measured beta values; black lines are group means")
    plt.show()
else:
    display(Markdown("The prepared beta matrix is unavailable. The saved per-site test results above remain viewable; run `make prepare` to enable the participant plots."))

Rerun, explore, and trace the sources¶

  • Explore: change SITE in section 9, or filter the results["before"] and results["after"] DataFrames. These tables contain every tested CpG.
  • Recompute the change test from saved shuffles: run make change-test (fast; no new shuffles).
  • Recompute the separate count tests from saved shuffles: run make count-test (fast; no new shuffles).
  • Choose a new example seed: run make plots EXAMPLE_SEED=70900, then make execute-notebook. With no seed option, later plot builds reuse the last selected seed.
  • Refresh this notebook and its HTML copy: run make execute-notebook from the project root.
  • Repeat the statistical analysis: use the commands in the README, including make corrections, make limma, and make permutation PERMUTATIONS=9999 SEED=70899. This can take several minutes and replaces generated outputs. Then run make plots and make execute-notebook.
  • Repeat the audit: with the full local matrix and R fits available, run make test and make audit. The corrected audit checks input hashes and the four-row patch, fits independent R models for selected corrected shuffles, and checks model symmetries and sample distances. Historical full source-value and replay checks are retained under results/audit/; make audit-deposited repeats those. Run OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=4 OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 .venv/bin/python scripts/audit_results.py --scenario corrected_visits --independent-seed 70901 to repeat the separate Monte Carlo check.
  • Read the implementation: limma model, joint shuffles, single-shuffle example, count test, change test, and numerical checks.

Primary sources: paper, public dataset, limma guide, minfi reference, Monte Carlo permutation p-values, permutation inference and exchangeability, and original trial allocation methods. Analysis commands default to corrected_visits. Explicit SCENARIO=deposited reruns the historical scenario and can overwrite its outputs. This notebook always reads the corrected scenario.
